items.paragraph: Batteries are often presented as the answer to the intermittency of wind and solar power: store the surplus when the sun shines and release it when it does not. items.paragraph: Seismologists distinguish between predicting an earthquake and forecasting one, and public discussion often blurs the two. A prediction would name a place, a window of days or weeks and a magnitude, precisely enough to justify evacuating a city. options.C: Modern states should learn from the fall of empires that expanding beyond their means invites collapse, and should keep their commitments within their capacities.
options.D: Great empires fall because they conquer more territory than they can defend or administer, so that the cost of their distant frontiers gradually drains the centre.

items.paragraph: A familiar account of why great empires fall points to overextension: they conquer more territory than they can defend or administer, and the cost of holding distant frontiers drains the centre. The account is attractive because it turns decline into a lesson about limits. Its weakness is that it is applied after the fact. Empires that collapsed are described as having overreached, while others that held equally vast and costly territories for centuries are not, and the difference is rarely explained by size alone. What seems to matter more is whether the centre could keep the loyalty of provincial elites and raise revenue without provoking revolt, capacities that some large empires possessed and some small ones lacked.

options.A: Before printing, scribes spelled words as they pronounced them, so that a manuscript produced in one town could look foreign to readers living in another.
options.B: Printing wiped out the regional dialects of written languages, because readers refused to buy books written in any variety other than the most widely spoken one.
options.C: Standard written languages were mainly created by scholars and rulers, who chose the most elegant regional varieties and then required printers to adopt them everywhere.
options.D: Printers' need for a form readable across large markets pushed written languages towards a standard that often reflected where presses clustered rather than its own merits.

items.paragraph: Before printing, a language written across a wide region existed in many local forms: scribes spelled as they spoke, and a manuscript copied in one town might look foreign in another. Printing changed the economics of this variety. A printer selling thousands of copies wanted a form of the language that readers across the whole market could follow, and once a few presses settled on particular spellings and grammar, every later book that followed them reinforced the choice. Standard written languages owe at least as much to this commercial pressure as to the decrees of scholars or rulers. The standard that emerged was not necessarily the most elegant or the most widely spoken variety; it was often simply the one used where the presses happened to cluster, and the dialects of other regions came to look like departures from a norm that was partly an accident of trade.

options.A: Argument cannot force anyone to enjoy something, yet disputes about taste remain worthwhile, because they draw attention to overlooked features and persuade by showing rather than by proof.
options.B: Since no argument can make anyone enjoy what they dislike, discussions about music or film are pointless exchanges of preference that reason is unable to touch.
options.C: Well-informed critics can, with enough patient explanation, eventually bring other people round to agreeing with their judgements about which films and music are good.
options.D: A slow opening in a film can be justified by the payoff it earns later, which an attentive viewer gradually learns to notice and to appreciate.

items.paragraph: It is often said that there is no disputing about taste, and in one sense this is right: no argument will make someone enjoy a dish they find bitter. Yet people argue about taste constantly, and not pointlessly. When a friend explains what to listen for in a piece of music, or why a film's slow opening earns its later payoff, she is not trying to overrule my pleasure by decree. She is directing my attention to features I may have missed, so that my next response is better informed. Such arguments cannot compel agreement, but they can change what there is to respond to. Taste is not beyond reason; it is simply reached by reasons of a different kind, ones that work by showing rather than by proving.

options.A: Nineteenth-century novelists often wrote carelessly because they were paid by the instalment, which accounts for the contrived plots and repetitive minor characters found in their books.
options.B: Modern readers ought to read nineteenth-century novels in monthly parts, as their first readers did, in order to appreciate their suspense and their characters.
options.C: Some features of serialised nineteenth-century novels that now look like flaws, such as cliffhanger endings and repeated character tags, were sensible responses to publication in instalments.
options.D: Serial publication let readers shape the plots of nineteenth-century novels, which authors rewrote every month according to what their audience demanded.

items.paragraph: Many nineteenth-century novels first reached readers in instalments, a part at a time over many months, and the form left marks on the books that later readers of the bound volume can miss. Each part needed its own small climax to bring buyers back, so chapters often close on suspense or revelation. Because readers might forget a minor character between instalments, writers gave such figures memorable tags, a phrase or a habit repeated at each appearance. The long gaps also let an author learn how the story was being received, and plots were sometimes adjusted in response. Features that a modern critic might fault as contrived or repetitive were, in their first setting, sensible answers to the conditions of publication.

options.A: Subscription firms often profit heavily from customers who keep paying out of postponement rather than choice, which is why critics stress easy cancelling over price.
options.B: Consumer advocates want every subscription service banned from charging customers who no longer make any use of the product they are paying for.
options.C: Subscription prices are deliberately set very high, since firms know that most customers rarely notice how much they are being charged each month.
options.D: Subscription services succeed because their customers enjoy them enough to keep paying month after month, whatever price the firm happens to charge them.

items.paragraph: Subscription businesses often earn much of their revenue not from enthusiastic users but from people who have stopped using the service and have not yet got round to cancelling it. Signing up is usually made quick and pleasant; cancelling is left to a later moment that never seems urgent, since each month's charge is small and easily overlooked. The firm benefits from a habit of postponement rather than from any decision to keep paying. This is why consumer advocates focus less on the price of subscriptions than on how easy they are to end.

options.A: Patients who take dummy pills in trials often report headaches, nausea and fatigue, which shows that most reported side effects of real drugs are imaginary.
options.B: Because warnings about side effects can produce the very symptoms they describe, doctors should generally avoid mentioning minor risks to those patients who seem anxious.
options.C: The nocebo effect is the counterpart of the placebo effect and arises because anxious patients notice ordinary bodily sensations that they would otherwise ignore.
options.D: Expecting side effects can produce symptoms, so doctors must disclose risks but should describe them in a way that informs without needless alarm.

items.paragraph: Patients in drug trials who receive only a dummy pill sometimes report the very side effects listed on the consent form: headaches, nausea, fatigue. This is the nocebo effect, the shadow of the better-known placebo effect. Expecting harm can produce real symptoms, partly because anxious attention makes people notice and interpret ordinary bodily sensations as signs of illness, and partly because worry itself can cause discomfort. The phenomenon puts doctors in an awkward position. They are obliged to warn patients about possible side effects, yet the way the warning is delivered may help bring those effects about. The aim is not to hide risks but to describe them in a way that informs without needlessly alarming.
